title: The COVID States Project #18: Fake news on Twitter (USA, October 2020)
screen_reason: Behavioural Twitter panel report: 1.6 million US registered voters matched to Twitter accounts, 29.7 million COVID-19 tweets (1 Jan - 30 Sep 2020), 7,062,989 of them containing a URL. It reports the share of shared COVID-19 URLs that come from fake news domains (1.1% for black+red domains, 1.8% when orange domains are added) plus by-party and by-age breakdowns of that share. A SHARING content_share with a stated denominator, so eligible.

estimates.measure_type: % of URLs shared in COVID-19 tweets that come from fake news domains (black + red domains)
estimates.value_raw: URLs from domains that publish fake news only comprise 1.1% of the URLs from COVID-19 tweets (vs 60% known reputable domains and 38.9% unknown quality)
estimates.denominator: All URLs shared in the 7,062,989 COVID-19 tweets (of 29,662,169) that contained at least one URL, posted by the 527,958 panel members who tweeted about COVID-19 out of a 1.6-million-account panel of registered US voters; each URL counted at most once per user; platform URLs (YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, etc.) removed
estimates.definition: URL whose web domain is on the 'black' or 'red' tier of the Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news domain classification - black = websites taken from preexisting lists of fake news sources; red = domains that spread falsehoods clearly reflecting a flawed editorial process. Classification is at domain level, so every URL from such a domain counts regardless of the content of the particular page.
estimates.misinfo_def: we define fake news as information that mirrors legitimate news in form, but “lacks the news media’s editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information.”
estimates.n: URLs in 7,062,989 COVID-19 tweets containing at least one URL
estimates.source_quote: In our panel, between January 1st and September 30th, 2020, the vast majority of shared URLs from COVID-19 tweets are either from known, reputable domains (60%), or domains with unknown quality (38.9%). URLs from domains that publish fake news only comprise 1.1% of the URLs from COVID-19 tweets.
estimates.page_loc: COVID-19 fake news sharing on Twitter, p. 4
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Grinberg et al. (2019, Science) three-tier fake-news domain list; black and red tiers treated as fake, orange excluded from the headline figure because those authors 'were less certain that the falsehoods stemmed from a systematically flawed process'. No per-URL verification; no reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: We retained only COVID-19 tweets by filtering using a broad list of 974 multi-lingual keywords, phrases and hashtags related to COVID-19. ... We correct for repeat sharers -- that is, people who share the same URL multiple times - by counting each URL at most one time per user, regardless of how many times they share it. We also remove URLs from platforms, such as YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, etc., so our sample contains mainly news domains.
estimates.notes: Headline poolable estimate. Denominator is COVID-19 URLs only (keyword-defined), not all tweets or all URLs, and it excludes platform URLs; the per-user URL de-duplication means this is a share of unique user-URL pairs rather than raw share events. The report itself calls 1.1% 'likely an underestimate'.

estimates.measure_type: % of URLs shared in COVID-19 tweets from fake news domains under the broader definition (black + red + orange domains)
estimates.value_raw: if we include web domains rated as “orange” in our fake news classification system, the percentage of shared fake news URLs increases to 1.8%
estimates.denominator: Same denominator: all URLs shared in the 7,062,989 COVID-19 tweets containing a URL, de-duplicated per user, platform URLs removed
estimates.definition: URL from a black, red OR orange domain in the Grinberg et al. classification; orange domains are those where the authors were less certain the falsehoods stemmed from a systematically flawed editorial process
estimates.misinfo_def: we define fake news as information that mirrors legitimate news in form, but “lacks the news media’s editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information.”
estimates.n: URLs in 7,062,989 COVID-19 tweets containing at least one URL
estimates.source_quote: However, this is likely an underestimate because if we include web domains rated as “orange” in our fake news classification system, the percentage of shared fake news URLs increases to 1.8%.
estimates.page_loc: COVID-19 fake news sharing on Twitter, p. 4
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Grinberg et al. (2019) domain list, all three tiers (black, red, orange)
estimates.moderator_quote: The fake news classifications were based on Grinberg et al, which has a three tier classification system for fake news domains: orange, red and black.
estimates.notes: Broader-definition variant of the 1.1% row; the same URLs and denominator, only the domain-list threshold changes. This pair is a clean illustration of how the source list drives the estimate (1.1% -> 1.8%).

estimates.measure_type: SUBGROUP: % of COVID-19 URLs shared by registered REPUBLICANS aged over 65 that come from fake news domains
estimates.value_raw: For those aged over 65, about 0.4% of the URLs shared by Democrats are from fake news domains; the corresponding numbers for Independents and Republicans are 3.7% and 5.3%, respectively
estimates.denominator: All COVID-19 URLs shared by panel members who are registered Republicans aged over 65 (subgroup of the 527,958 COVID-19 tweeters)
estimates.definition: URL from a black or red Grinberg et al. fake-news domain, among URLs shared by this age x party subgroup
estimates.misinfo_def: we define fake news as information that mirrors legitimate news in form, but “lacks the news media’s editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information.”
estimates.source_quote: For those aged over 65, about 0.4% of the URLs shared by Democrats are from fake news domains; the corresponding numbers for Independents and Republicans are 3.7% and 5.3%, respectively.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Grinberg et al. (2019) black+red domain list; party from voter-file registration matched to the Twitter panel, age from the same voter-file match
estimates.moderator_quote: We find that registered Republicans share proportionally more URLs from fake news domains than registered Democrats and Independents (see Figure 3), which is true for all age groups.
estimates.notes: SUBGROUP row (party x age), recorded because who shares fake news by party is this report's headline finding. Do NOT pool with the 1.1% overall row - it is conditional on both party (Republican) and age (65+), the two-way cell with the highest value. Subgroup denominators are not reported.

estimates.measure_type: SUBGROUP: % of COVID-19 URLs shared by registered DEMOCRATS aged over 65 that come from fake news domains
estimates.value_raw: For those aged over 65, about 0.4% of the URLs shared by Democrats are from fake news domains
estimates.denominator: All COVID-19 URLs shared by panel members who are registered Democrats aged over 65
estimates.definition: URL from a black or red Grinberg et al. fake-news domain, among URLs shared by this age x party subgroup
estimates.misinfo_def: we define fake news as information that mirrors legitimate news in form, but “lacks the news media’s editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information.”
estimates.source_quote: For those aged over 65, about 0.4% of the URLs shared by Democrats are from fake news domains; the corresponding numbers for Independents and Republicans are 3.7% and 5.3%, respectively.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Grinberg et al. (2019) black+red domain list; party and age from the voter-file match
estimates.moderator_quote: We find that registered Republicans share proportionally more URLs from fake news domains than registered Democrats and Independents (see Figure 3), which is true for all age groups.
estimates.notes: SUBGROUP row (party x age), the low end of the party contrast reported in the same sentence as the Republican 5.3%. Value is prefixed 'about' in the source. Do NOT pool with the 1.1% overall row.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Not extracted (subgroup, and third value of the same sentence): Independents aged over 65, 3.7% of shared URLs from fake domains. (2) Not extracted: the age gradient for political independents - 0.2% (18-29), 0.7% (30-49), 1.7% (50-64), 3.7% (65+) of shared URLs from fake domains - age subgroups within one party, all conditional cells. (3) Not extracted: per-capita SHARING intensities - independents shared 5.7 / 12.4 / 27.7 / 54.1 COVID-19 URLs per capita by age band, and 0.01 / 0.09 / 0.48 / 1.98 FAKE NEWS URLs per capita by age band. These are per_capita_intensity values but only for one party's age bands, with no overall per-capita figure given. (4) Not extracted: Gateway Pundit shares - 7.6 per 1,000 COVID-19 URLs in March rising to 12.1 per 1,000 in September, and rank 4th/6th most-shared domain of ALL domains in August/September. This is the closest thing to a CONCENTRATION statement (one domain's share of all sharing) but it fails R1 because no group size as a % of sources is given. Flag for the adjudicator: 12.1 per 1,000 = 1.21% of September COVID URLs from a single fake domain sits oddly against the 1.1% all-fake-domain figure for the whole Jan-Sep period - most likely because fake-news sharing rose over the period and/or because the per-1000 series is not de-duplicated per user; the report does not reconcile them. (5) Not extracted: belief figures (Democrats 18-29 believe 1.92 of 11 pieces of COVID misinformation, Democrats 65+ 0.87; Republicans 2.26 and 1.21) - belief, excluded, and in any case imported from COVID States report #14. (6) Figures 1-6 carry most of the age x party grid and are not present in this text file, so further cell values exist that could not be read.

rob.design: Behavioural panel: 1.6 million Twitter accounts matched to US voter-file records (TargetSmart) carrying age, race, gender and party registration; COVID-19 tweets identified with 974 multilingual keywords/phrases/hashtags matched in tweet text, quoted text, hashtags or URL string (not the linked page content), 1 Jan - 30 Sep 2020; 527,958 accounts tweeted about COVID-19, giving 29,662,169 COVID-19 tweets of which 7,062,989 contained at least one URL. URLs classified at DOMAIN level using Grinberg et al. (2019) black/red/orange tiers (black+red = fake in the headline figure); each URL counted at most once per user to correct for repeat sharers; platform domains (YouTube, Facebook, Instagram) removed. Analyses on aggregate data, protocols reviewed by Northeastern University's IRB. Non-peer-reviewed consortium report (Report #18, v.1, 21 October 2020), NSF-funded. No accuracy or reliability statistics for the domain classification; the panel is registered voters with public Twitter accounts, not a representative sample of Americans or of Twitter users.
rob.item6_quote: Social media acts as a conduit for fake news websites, where we define fake news as information that mirrors legitimate news in form, but “lacks the news media’s editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information.”
rob.item10_quote: Of the 29,662,169 COVID-19 tweets in our panel, 7,062,989 contained at least one URL. ... URLs from domains that publish fake news only comprise 1.1% of the URLs from COVID-19 tweets.
